items.title: DeepSeek-V4.1 on the native engine: one family, CUDA and Metal (tracker)
items.body:
Thank you to everyone who has put work into DeepSeek-V4.1 on the native engine. @jayleaton's CUDA stack (#635 to #727) is the most complete community port we've had. @akol1 brought the Metal family (#824 to #827) and proposed the layout on #635. @bertholomus and @ecohash-co's port (#559) has served real traffic on four GB10s, and their updates there are some of the most careful measurement anyone has posted here.

This issue is where those pieces come together, the way #832 does for EXL3.

**The plan**

- One family package, `zig/src/families/deepseek_v41/`, with no backend code in it: configuration, weight and pack loading, the Engram tables and token map, cache and history state, and round planning. This is the split @akol1 proposed on #635.
- Kernels beside it: Metal in `zig/kernels/metal/deepseek_v41/`, CUDA in `zig/kernels/cuda/deepseek_v41/`.
- Each backend implements the lane core's `Backend`. Drafts, the prompt cache and concurrency come from the core, so on every backend drafted output equals `"draft": false`, a resumed prompt equals a fresh one, and concurrent equals solo.
- EXL3 goes through the one EXL3 module (#832). The Metal projection and the CUDA linear and grouped experts become that module's backends.
- The default boot needs no capture directory. Captured Triton cubins can stay an optional input, in the layout the 27B's capture already uses (`packaging/README.md`).
- Carried kernels keep their attribution, and their authors get Co-authored-by lines. We add those when the code lands.

**Where the trees differ today**

- Both write `config.zig`, `load.zig`, `model.zig` and `kv_state.zig` under `zig/src/families/deepseek_v41/`, with different contents. Each becomes one file.
- #827's lane backend runs with drafts off (`backend.zig:58` and `:63`). It lands once it decodes with drafts on and passes its whole-model gate.
- The CUDA layers need one GPU run at the current heads, as asked on #635.

**Order**

1. The shared pieces, each as its own increment with our gate, as described on #635: #635, #636, #637, #662, #663.
2. The family package, agreed here.
3. The CUDA backend from #667 to #727 and the Metal backend from #824 to #827, each through its own gates.

**Open questions**

- @akol1's three questions on #635. Our answer to the third: served-side state lives in the family package. On the first, we'd rather have one loader whose plan becomes rank 0 of 1 on a Mac, if that fits both backends.
- Credit. 18 of the CUDA kernel files say they are copies of `src/tensorfold/families/deepseek_v41/cuda/`, and one of `src/tensorfold/families/glm5_next/spark/`. Neither path is in TensorFold's Python line (v0.6.6 has `deepseek_v4`). Whose tree are they from, and who wrote them? Their authors get the same credit as everyone else.
- KV formats. #827 keeps the window and main caches in fp8 and fp4. If DeepSeek's reference keeps them that way, please link it. Otherwise bf16 is the default, with lower precision behind an opt-in flag.

Please comment here with anything that changes the plan.

items.title: GLM-5.3-Flash and full GLM-5.3 on the native CUDA engine (tracker)
items.body:
This issue collects all the GLM work on the native CUDA engine in one place. Eight threads asked overlapping questions about the same port: #509, #552, #402, #310, #308, #214, #339 and #566. Each is closed with a link here, and its proposals and receipts stay readable there. Please post claims, plans and receipts here, so two people don't build the same piece.

## Where things stand

- Native CUDA serves Nemotron 3.5 Lightning only. The native GLM family serves GLM-5.3-Flash on Metal.
- Several working GLM-5.3-Flash CUDA ports exist outside the tree: @MiaAI-Lab's EXL3 port at TP=2 on two GB10s ([their recipe](https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold), greedy replies with drafts off equal to the Python engine token for token), @Bizuayeu's TP=2 port over NCCL (#339, #548), and our own MLX affine 4-bit port, in progress.
- Shared CUDA layers are coordinated in #548. #587 (one quantized-weight interface, `qlinear.zig`) is in review, and the NVFP4 entry follows it.

## The gate

Every PR here passes the same gate as the rest of the engine:
- drafted equal to `"draft": false`, resumed equal to fresh, concurrent equal to solo, on the device;
- an FP64 reference for every projection class whose reduction order changes, with worst-column errors;
- prefill and decode measured against the current release and against vLLM on the same hardware;
- bf16 KV, and no arithmetic below today's precision;
- drafts and concurrency through the lane core, with no serial serving path;
- files under 600 lines, one-line comments, and no Python in the engine or its tools.
Bit equality with the Python engine is not required.

## The pieces, in order

1. Shared layers (#548): the quantized-weight interface (#587), then NVFP4 behind it, including grouped NVFP4 experts on prompt rows.
2. Multi-rank communication: `zig/src/cuda/nccl.zig` has AllReduce, AllGather and Broadcast. Send/recv and an exact reduce-scatter in rank order (#310's) come as one small PR.
3. The GLM-5.3-Flash family on one GPU, then TP=2 and TP=3 with #310's unequal shares. Any of the ports above can be the first PR. Whichever passes the gate first lands, and the others build on it. Say here before you open one.
4. Checkpoint formats on that family: MLX affine 4-bit, EXL3 on the reference decoder from #496, and NVIDIA's NVFP4 checkpoint read as stored, W4A16 (#308).
5. Full GLM-5.3 (`glm_moe_dsa`) as its own family that reuses the Flash family's CUDA pieces rather than copying them: TP=3 (#402) and TP=4 (#552).
6. Later, on top: the heat wait on GLM prefill under the engine's `TF_HEAT_HIGH` and `TF_HEAT_LOW` (#339), DFlash2 drafts (#509), attention on a desktop GPU with routed experts on the Sparks (#214), and Living Weights for GLM-5.3-Flash on CUDA (#566, after #591).

## Answers to #552's questions

1. Yes, a `glm_moe_dsa` family is wanted, sharing the Flash family's pieces as in step 5. Who is doing what is listed above.
2. NCCL, which the CUDA engine already uses. The cluster layer's links are built for the Macs' Thunderbolt RDMA. A `TF_NCCL_LIB` override for hosts without a system NCCL is fine.
3. The gate above. Bit equality with the Python engine is not required.
4. Hand-written `.cu`. 1.0.3 moved Nemotron to our own CUDA kernels, and new families follow.
5. Yes, bf16 KV. An FP8 KV cache, such as #509's `fp8_ds_mla` layout, would trade precision, so it isn't on the default path.
6. Yes, a tiny synthetic checkpoint for host tests is welcome, made by a Zig tool in the tree.

items.title: Gemma 4 on Macs: the dense 31B, the 12B (`gemma4_unified`) with its MTP assistant, and oQ mixed widths?
items.body:
## The question

The `gemma4` family serves the 26B-A4B MoE checkpoints at uniform 4-bit with an 8-bit router. TensorFold refuses
three other Gemma 4 cases today:

- the dense **31B** (`model_type: gemma4`, `enable_moe_block: false`);
- the **12B**, which ships as `Gemma4UnifiedForConditionalGeneration` (`model_type: gemma4_unified`) with a separate
  MTP assistant (`gemma4_unified_assistant`);
- every **oMLX oQ/oQe checkpoint** of any size, whose `config.json` sets widths per layer.

Would you take Mac support for these, under the exactness contract? And should the dense paths live inside `gemma4`,
or should the 12B be its own family?

## What it would take

- **Dense layers (31B and 12B).** `RowDecode` runs the dense layout with the existing `attn_tail`, the stacked GeGLU
  gate/up, the down projection, and one new kernel, `dense_tail`. That kernel is `moe_tail`'s arithmetic with the MLP
  output in place of the joined branches: post-feedforward norm, residual, layer scalar, and the next layer's input
  norm.
- **Mixed widths.** Projections read every MLX affine width the existing kernels read (2–8 bits in groups of
  32/64/128): the 4-bit row matvec, `qwen.dense.v1.affine_rows` for other widths, and the lane matmul where it reads
  the width. A stack whose members differ in width (oQ boosts one of q/k/v or gate/up) runs one matmul per run of
  equal widths and joins the outputs. Every kernel is row-invariant, so windows, shared rounds and one-row steps keep
  the same bits. The router may be any width; experts stay 4-bit. `check` refuses, by tensor name, any width, group or
  mode no kernel reads.
- **The 12B.**
  - **Text only.** Prompts run mlx-lm's `gemma4` forward, with the patch embedder and audio projection dropped at
    load.
  - **Decode** runs Gemma 4's v1 attention, RoPE and caches with the dense tail above.
  - **Drafts** come from the `gemma4_unified_assistant` head: four layers attending over the target's last sliding and
    last full layer's keys from the last kept row, batched across streams in shared rounds. Drafts only propose, so
    the assistant runs MLX's stock kernels.
  - `check` refuses the other Gemma 4 layouts this path does not read: MoE, per-layer input, shared KV.
- **Memory.** On the rows backend the stacked q/k/v and gate/up become views into mlx_lm's modules, so a stack costs
  no second copy.

## What it does not change

The uniform 4-bit 26B-A4B checkpoint keeps its kernels: a 4-bit run still takes the fused q/k/v row kernel.

## Measured so far (our own scripts, not yet the upstream tools)

M5 Ultra, MLX 0.32.3, greedy, 512-token replies. In every case, drafted replies equal `"draft": false`, and two- and
four-stream replies equal serial ones, by token hash.

| checkpoint (ours, oMLX `oq`, groups of 64) | single stream | aggregate | prompt |
|---|---|---|---|
| 26B-A4B oQ4e (4-bit base with 5/6/8-bit layers, experts 4-bit) | 177 tok/s undrafted; 187–193 with `z-lab/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-DFlash` | — | — |
| 31B oQ8e (uniform 8-bit) | 40 tok/s with a DFlash drafter | 83 at four streams (lane backend) | — |
| 12B oQ8e + `mlx-community/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-assistant-4bit` | 131.7 tok/s drafted, 52.0 undrafted | 238.7 at four streams | about 2.9–3.2K tok/s |

The three checkpoints are published as `unigilby/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-oQ4e`, `unigilby/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-oQ8e`
and `unigilby/gemma-4-12B-it-oQ8e`. They use oMLX `oq` (enhanced) with groups of 64, and one width per q/k/v and
gate/up stack. Other oQ/oQe packs of Gemma 4, whose stacks mix widths, load too: the mixed-width runs above read them.

## Questions

1. **One family or two?** Dense layers inside `gemma4` (the 31B), and the 12B as its own `gemma4_unified` family
   reusing them? Or one dense path for both inside `gemma4`?
2. **Checkpoints.** The families' `MODELS` would name our published packs above. Would you rather `TensorFold/`
   host copies, as it does for its other models?

We have both branches ready and would open them after your answer.

items.title: Zig ROCM: RDNA2/3/3.5/4 and more integration
items.body:
Goal of the issue is to track the integration of RDNA devices into tensorfold as several PR have been made to the previous python version #389 #144 #412.

I previously discussed trying to make something additive to @ThinkOffApp work in #463 but since I have a working structure in #490 as well this issue is the opportunity to discuss both structures and make the best of both worlds to facilitate models, kernels and rdna devices integration. My PR is only meant as a draft, since it needs to be split in several PRs.




## Proposed structure

The idea is to keep #463 as the runtime and build the rest on top of it, in this order:

1. Runtime (#463): loading HIP, memory, streams, modules, launches. I can add gfx1030 and gfx1100 runs, and a few fixes as a PR to that branch.
2. Caps table: what each GPU can do, read from its gfx name.
3. Kernels: one tile written once and specialized per format, activation type and instruction, a registry that picks a kernel per shape from a per-GPU tuning table, all checked against an fp64 reference.
4. Model family (Qwen3.5 MLX affine) on the shared lane core: graphs, MTP, radix prompt cache.
5. Tensor parallel over RCCL.

## Caps table

RDNA GPUs differ in a few things that decide how a kernel is written: wave size, which dot instructions exist (f16, bf16, int8), whether there are matrix cores and which generation, and whether activations are fp16 or bf16. Instead of checking GPU names in the code, the idea is one table that maps a gfx name to these capabilities:

| family | gfx | wave | dot2 | matrix cores | activations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RDNA2 | gfx1030-1036 | 32 | f16 | none | fp16 |
| RDNA3 | gfx1100-1103 | 32 | f16, bf16 | WMMA | bf16 |
| RDNA3.5 | gfx1150-1153 | 32 | f16, bf16 | WMMA | bf16 |
| RDNA4 | gfx1200-1201 | 32 | f16, bf16 | WMMA (gfx12) | bf16 |

- The runtime reads the gfx name at startup and looks it up; an unknown GPU is refused instead of guessed.
- Kernels are compiled with the caps as macros and choose instructions from them, so the same source builds for every row.
- The kernel registry picks a kernel per shape from the caps and a small per-GPU tuning file.
- A new GPU in a known family is one row; a new instruction is one new kernel variant, not a fork of the code.
- The build takes a list or a family (`-Dgfx=rdna2,rdna3,rdna3.5`).

A runtime-only version with this table is in #492 (tested on gfx1030 and gfx1100), for comparison with #463.

Measured on 1× NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB), TensorFold 0.6.5 (`--parallel 5 --kv-dtype int8 --mtp-drafts 6`), checkpoint `Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, against vLLM (MiaAI-Lab single-Spark recipe, same checkpoint, `MAX_NUM_SEQS 6`) on an identical second Spark. We know the Python engine is frozen at 0.6.5 (#286): we post this as input for the Zig CUDA server. Bench scripts and raw results will be public shortly; happy to share them now or run any build on our two Sparks.

**Use case.** One-token decisions after reasoning (« think, then answer A/B/C ») need `top_logprobs` (up to 20) of the first token of the visible answer. On 0.6.5 CUDA, `logprobs` with thinking on returns 400 (`src/tensorfold/cuda/server.py:254-256`), although the engine already takes logprobs from the verified target logits (`decode.py:474-476`, `cuda/logprobs.py:31`); only the split between reasoning and answer was missing.

**Reference implementation (0.6.5, 5 files, +78/−17).** Logprobs are kept only after the first `</think>` (and the `\n\n` that follows), so `content[0]` is the answer token; a reply cut inside reasoning returns `[]`; streaming, tools, `stop` and `response_format` stay refused with thinking on. items.title: CUDA graphs: collectives inside a captured step cost ~10 us more on GB10; split at collectives and share captured steps across sequences
items.body:
Two findings from the Zig CUDA Flash Next port on two GB10s (context in #472) that apply to any CUDA family that captures decode steps as graphs. That's Nemotron today (`nemotron/cuda_engine.zig`, `cuda_mtp.zig`), and the multi-rank ports in flight. This issue is to agree on whether and where the helpers should live before any PR.

**1. A collective inside a captured graph costs about 10 us more than eager.** Time per partial-sum all-gather between two GB10 ranks over RoCE (NCCL 2.30.7):

| Rows | Eager | Inside one graph | Graph ended at the gather, gather eager |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (10 KiB a rank) | 15.9 us | 25.1 us | 15.4 us |
| 6 (60 KiB) | 37.6 us | 44.3 us | 37.3 us |
| 16 (160 KiB) | 33.1 us | 43.8 us | 34.9 us |

- Tried without gain: `NCCL_PROTO` (`LL` is much worse at 16 rows), channel counts, and graph registration off.
- `NCCL_GRAPH_MIXING_SUPPORT=0` brings graphs close to eager, but it isn't safe when a process mixes graph and eager collectives, as a server with eager prompt passes does.
- What worked: end each captured segment at a collective, and launch the collective eager between segments. The payload, the sum and its order are unchanged.

**2. One captured step can serve every sequence.** Keying graphs by sequence means each new request captures its own: 36-41 a request in our case, at 3-7 ms each. Instead:
- At capture, read each kernel node's argument layout (`cuFuncGetParamInfo`, or `cuKernelGetParamInfo` for library kernels). Note the 8-byte words that point into the capturing sequence's allocations, as offsets from their base.
- At launch for another sequence, rewrite only those words (`cuGraphExecKernelNodeSetParams`), and only when the bound bases differ.
- Copy and memset nodes are checked the same way. A node that can't be relocated, NCCL's included, keeps the plan per sequence. Plans are LRU-capped at 96.

Sharing gained nothing while the collectives sat inside the graphs (those plans can't move), but on top of 1 it took requests to 0-9 captures.

**Measured together** (Flash Next TP2, greedy, 256-token replies, the same checkpoint and settings, outputs bit-identical):
- one stream: 66.8 / 106.1 / 85.1 / 106.9 tok/s before, 77.1 / 125.7 / 99.1 / 125.7 after (+15-21%), the same after other traffic;
- 4-16 streams unchanged.

Exactness on both ranks, at int8 and int4 caches:
- the reply equals the Python engine's;
- shared rounds and batched prompts equal each stream alone;
- resumed equals fresh;
- drafted equals undrafted.

The code is on https://github.com/BobClawblaw/TensorFold/tree/native-v1.0.4: `zig/src/cuda/graph.zig` and `abi.zig` (node getters, param info, exec node set), and `families/flashnext_cuda/plan.zig` (split points, relocation).

Related, for anyone caching graphs per sequence: free a sequence's graphs when it's released. Pooled spares and kept prompt states otherwise pile them up (161 graphs over 9 sequences after a few minutes of mixed traffic), captures slow down, and one stream lost 7-10% until a restart.

**Questions:**
- Should the split-at-collective capture and the relocatable plan be shared helpers in `cuda/graph.zig`, landing with the first upstream family that uses them (Nemotron's MTP or verify steps, or a multi-rank port)? Or should each family keep its own?
- For the gate, is the existing contract enough (bit-identical replies, drafted equals undrafted, concurrent equals solo, resumed equals fresh), plus a before/after with the receipts CONTRIBUTING asks for?

items.title: Jetson AGX Thor (sm_110): measurements and questions for a Flash Next NVFP4 prompt path on 0.6.0
items.body:
TensorFold 0.6.0 is running on my Jetson AGX Thor (compute capability 11.0, 20 SMs). An agent took the measurements below on that machine. I approved posting them. I have not line-reviewed the code.

With `local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (rev `7c4f1bc1`), 0.6.0 serves the full 262,144-token window at `--parallel 4` and int8 KV (gate run r12). Thank you.

A local branch adds a Thor prompt path on 0.6.0. Before any larger pull request, I would like guidance on structure. 128 GB and 273 GB/s are the published Thor specs; they were not re-measured in these runs.

## Stock 0.6.0 on Thor

The gate bench, first requests counted, `--kv-dtype int8 --parallel 4`, full window (run r12):

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Prefill 8k / 32k / 128k tokens | 926 / 899 / 798 tok/s |
| One-user decode | 36.7 tok/s |
| Combined decode at 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 users | 34.8 / 53.7 / 70.3 / 76.7 tok/s |
| First answer to a 60k-token prompt | 69.7 s |

One-user decode is already close to vLLM's FP8 build on this box, which decodes at 38.4 tok/s. Prefill is the gap: vLLM's FP8 build prefills 2,101 tok/s at 32k.

Thor is datacenter Blackwell (tcgen05 tensor cores, like B200), not consumer Blackwell like the Spark. cuBLAS picks sm_110 tcgen05 kernels, and several of FlashInfer's SM100 CuTe DSL kernels run on it unchanged. The block-scaled MMA does not compile for sm_110a in CuTe DSL 4.8.

## What is built so far

Items 1 and 2, and the GDN chain in item 4, are behind an sm_110 check with a kill switch, so other GPUs never reach them; item 3 is two small fixes for every CUDA GPU. Items 1 and 2 passed these gates before they were counted:

- **G-A accuracy:** against an fp32 or fp64 reference on real checkpoint weights, at 128 / 512 / 2048 / 4096 rows; the error must be at most 1.5x TensorFold's own.
- **G-B equivalence:** greedy output on 6 long and 4 short prompts; every divergence must be explained to the token.
- **Invariants:** solo == concurrent, drafted == serial and resend == fresh, on a running server.
- **G-C speed:** the end-to-end bench, against stock in the same session.
- **G-D memory:** KV room, context window and the startup estimate.

**1. Routed NVFP4 experts on FlashInfer's W4A16 grouped GEMM**

This uses FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1's CuTe DSL `Sm100W4A16GroupedGemmKernel`. It decodes the NVFP4 weights exactly to bf16 in shared memory and runs bf16 tcgen05 MMAs with fp32 sums. Gated run r09, against stock r10 in the same session:

| Metric | Stock (r10) | Thor path (r09) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prefill 8k / 32k / 128k | 925 / 900 / 801 tok/s | 1,295 / 1,261 / 1,075 tok/s | +40 / +40 / +34% |
| One-user decode | 37.7 tok/s | 39.7 tok/s | +5% |
| Combined decode at 1-4 users | | | +7 / +10 / +6 / +6% |
| First answer at 60k | 69.1 s | 50.1 s | -27% |

- **Accuracy:** 66/66 cells at 0.64-0.75x TensorFold's own error. That ratio is the previous gate (r08), carried into r09.
- **Equivalence:** 6 of 10 outputs are byte-identical; the other 4 diverge at bf16-step ties.
- **Invariants:** pass.
- **Memory:** 0.7 GiB less KV room; the window is unchanged.

This path calls FlashInfer's internal runner, because the public entry lists CC 100/103/107. A small FlashInfer PR adding SM110 for W4A16 is open: flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5882.

Related: #173 asks about FP4 activations for these experts on the Spark. This path keeps bf16 activations, like the current kernel.

**2. Dense prompt GEMMs on cuBLAS bf16**

MXFP8 values are exact in bf16, so the DeltaNet and attention projections, the shared expert and the other dense prompt GEMMs run as cuBLAS bf16 GEMMs over exact weights, with fp32 sums. Decode keeps your kernels. This includes item 1 and stage-ahead (below). Gated run r11, against stock r12:

| Metric | Stock (r12) | Thor path (r11) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prefill 8k / 32k / 128k | 926 / 899 / 798 tok/s | 1,658 / 1,549 / 1,261 tok/s | +79 / +72 / +58% |
| Natural-text 32k prefill | 859 tok/s | 1,405 tok/s | +64% |
| First answer at 60k | 69.7 s | 41.6 s | -40% |
| 3-user decode (`decode3`, separate from the combined-concurrency row) | 66.1 tok/s | 76.3 tok/s | +15% |
| One-user decode | 36.7 tok/s | 36.9 tok/s | held |

- **Accuracy:** 99/99 cells at 1.000x TensorFold's error.
- **Equivalence:** 4 divergences, each a bf16-step near-tie, checked against an exact-GEMM referee. The gate note says four prompts do not separate the two paths, and a wider set was still pending.
- **Memory:** 0.7 GiB less KV room.

Each MXFP8 weight can be dequantized at every call, as in r11, or kept as a bf16 copy. In one same-process run, not gated (`kprof-k2r1`), the copies were 1.8-2.9% faster depending on length. Startup logs (`k2c-c1`) show 5.47 GiB of copies and cache room 26.0 GiB against 31.5 GiB, at 4.47 GiB for one full window, which is 5 streams against 7. The local branch currently keeps the copies unless a switch selects dequant.

**3. Two generic fixes**

These are open as separate small PRs, #201 and #202, measured on stock 0.6.0:
- reading a prompt pass's n-gram rows before waiting on the previous step's copies;
- building the CUDA extensions before the weights load. On unified memory, a first start that built them after the load had 1.4-2 GiB less MemAvailable than the next start, still missing 20 s after the server came up. Built before the load, the same builds left 0.01-0.15 GiB, about the noise between two starts.

**4. Open work**

- **GDN prompt chain.** Not gated. On top of the expert and dense path, one same-process run (`k4g-f1`) cut in-situ GDN time at 32k by 3.11x, and synthetic 32k prefill rose about 15% (1,501 to 1,728 tok/s).
  - A chunked chain's bits depend on its 64-row chunk grid.
  - The branch keeps your invariants by putting kept points and prompt pieces on that grid below 32k rows. Past 32k it runs your chain, because the fp16 state drifts over long prompts.
  - That changes where prompts are kept, so I'd like your view before proposing it (question 3 below).
- **Sparse attention (QSA) prompt kernels.** Next on the list: attention is now the largest share of a 32k prefill.

At 32k the branch is at 74% of vLLM's FP8 prefill (1,549 against 2,101 tok/s, r11 and r01). The target is 3-5k tok/s.

## Proposal

1. **Small PRs.** Upstream the Thor path as small PRs, each behind an sm_110 check and a kill switch:
   - the routed experts;
   - the dense prompt GEMMs;
   - later, GDN and QSA.

   Each PR keeps your exactness invariants and brings its tests (`tests/cuda`, skipped unless sm_110) and its measurements.
2. If a Thor path is welcome, I'd like to help keep it working, and can run the Thor tests above before releases.

## Questions

1. **Where should architecture-specific kernels live?**
   - Today they are `cuda/nvfp4/thor_experts.py`, `cuda/nvfp4/thor_dense.py` and `cuda/kernels/thor_gdn.py`.
   - The switches are `TENSORFOLD_THOR_*`. Should they follow your `TF_*` naming?
2. **Is an optional FlashInfer dependency acceptable?** NVIDIA's Jetson containers ship FlashInfer; it would be imported only on sm_110, and the portable kernels would run without it. If not, would you prefer vendored or JIT-built kernels?
3. **For chunked kernels (GDN, and possibly attention), is "bit-identical on the 64-row grid" acceptable?**
   - That means kept points and pieces aligned to 64 rows, so resumes and concurrent prompts keep their bits.
   - Or do you want every prompt kernel to stay row-exact at any split?
4. **Is there anything coming in 0.6.x that would change this?**
   - The 0.6.1 branch (#141) reworks prompt fills and kept points in `multi.py`. The two small patches merge onto it with no conflict markers and were not tested there.

Thanks!

---

*Sources:*
- *r08-r12 are gated runs on this Jetson AGX Thor (the TensorFold 0.6.0 tag plus the named changes), with `local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` rev `7c4f1bc1`.*
- *The vLLM figures are run r01: NVIDIA's Jetson vLLM image with the FP8-hybrid recipe on the same Thor.*
- *Lines marked "not gated" come from same-process A/B runs or startup logs (run labels in parentheses), without the full gate set.*

AI disclosure: an AI coding agent (Claude Code) wrote this issue and the Thor changes it describes, and ran the measurements on my Jetson AGX Thor. I approved posting it; I have not reviewed the code line by line.

items.title: [CUDA vision] Mia Qwen3.8 Flash Next NVFP4 checkpoint fails to start with --vision on v0.6.1
items.body:
### Summary

TensorFold v0.6.1 serves text from the `Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` checkpoint on an NVIDIA DGX Spark, but the same checkpoint does not start with `--vision`.

The v0.6.1 CUDA recipe lists this Mia checkpoint for Flash Next. On the unmodified v0.6.1 checkout, startup first rejects the checkpoint's top-level `model_type=qwen3_8_flash_next` and nested vision type `qwen3_5_vision`. After adding those aliases to the relevant vision-family checks, startup proceeds further and fails while validating a quantized vision tensor:

```text
ValueError: invalid or unsupported vision tensor range: blocks.0.mlp.linear_fc2.weight_scale_2
```

Text-only serving works with this checkpoint. This report is specifically about enabling image input for its NVFP4-quantized vision tower.

### Environment

- TensorFold tag: `v0.6.1`
- Upstream tag commit: `17c73e189f5e6a5304cda7ea37f086f9c49b4788`
- Host: NVIDIA DGX Spark, GB10, Linux ARM64
- Container: NVIDIA PyTorch `26.07-py3`, Torch `2.13.0a0+9186a08.nv26.07`, CUDA 13.3
- Checkpoint: [`Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`](https://huggingface.co/Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4)
- Checkpoint revision: `925d7be6c14c6c9442ef83e8f05b5a3c39304f69`
- `transformers`: 5.18.0

The host driver was 580.126.09, so the container reported CUDA minor-version compatibility mode.

### Reproduction

With the pinned checkpoint present locally, run the v0.6.1 CUDA server with `--vision` (representative options used in the test):

```bash
tensorfold serve /path/to/Mia-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 \
  --backend cuda \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8888 \
  --name qwen3.8-flash-next \
  --context 262144 \
  --temperature 0.1 \
  --top-p 0.8 \
  --top-k 20 \
  --min-p 0 \
  --no-prefill-fp8 \
  --no-drafts \
  --kv-dtype int8 \
  --vision \
  --parallel 2 \
  --no-update-check
```

On the stock v0.6.1 checkout, compatibility checks reject the model/vision aliases before weights are loaded. After adding `qwen3_8_flash_next` to the relevant top-level model allowlists and `qwen3_5_vision` to the CUDA vision-family check, startup reaches the checkpoint reader but exits with the tensor error above. No changes were made to tensor validation or quantization handling.

### Checkpoint tensor metadata

For `model.visual.blocks.0.mlp.linear_fc2`, the safetensors header reports:

| Tensor | Dtype | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `weight` | `U8` | `[1152, 2152]` |
| `weight_scale` | `F8_E4M3` | `[1152, 269]` |
| `weight_scale_2` | `F32` | scalar `[]` |
| `bias` | `BF16` | `[1152]` |

This appears to be an NVFP4-quantized visual projection with auxiliary scale tensors. The current vision reader rejects the scalar `weight_scale_2` as an unsupported visual tensor range. I have not tried relaxing that check or converting the tensor, since that would not establish correct NVFP4 dequantization or image results.

### Expected behavior

If image input for this NVFP4 checkpoint is intended to be supported in v0.6.1, the CUDA vision loader should recognize the checkpoint's vision architecture and load its quantized projection plus scale tensors with the correct NVFP4 math. A small real-image request should then return a useful answer through `/v1/chat/completions`.

If the vision tower is not supported, it would help to clarify that the listed Flash Next NVFP4 checkpoint is currently text-only with `--vision`, or document which visual checkpoint/precision is required.

### Additional observations

- The same checkpoint starts and serves text when `--vision` is omitted.
- The vision startup failure occurs before the HTTP server becomes ready; no image request can be submitted.
- A local alias-only compatibility patch passed its targeted unit tests, but did not address the NVFP4 tensor failure.
- Drafting was disabled (`--no-drafts`) and `DRAFT_LANGUAGE` was empty; no MTP vocabulary was installed or enabled.

The v0.6.1 CUDA recipe referenced above lists the Mia-AiLab Flash Next NVFP4 checkpoint: <https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.1/docs/recipes/cuda.md>.

items.title: CUDA Flash Next: one image in an agent chat makes every later turn re-prefill the whole conversation (~190k tokens, cached_tokens=0)
items.body:
## Summary

On CUDA (Qwen3.8 Flash Next, one DGX Spark), once a single image enters an agent conversation, **every following turn re-prefills the whole conversation from token 0**, because the image stays in the history. In a long agent session this turns ~1–10 s turns into ~2 min turns for the rest of the session.

This is the same limitation reported for GLM-5.3 / Mac in #388 and #314 (and MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold#37). Filing separately to confirm it also hits **CUDA Flash Next**, with numbers from a real agent session.

## Setup

- TensorFold **v0.6.1** (`17c73e1`) via [MiaAI-Lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Single-DGX-Spark-TensorFold](https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Single-DGX-Spark-TensorFold) recipe defaults (image `v0.6.1-797af1d9df4d`)
- Model `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP`, `--parallel 5 --context 262144 --kv-dtype int8 --vision --ple-on-ssd`
- Client: pi coding agent over `/v1/chat/completions`; a browser tool returns screenshots as `image_url` parts inside tool results
- One conversation, no other clients sending requests at the time

## What happens

`usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` per request (from the client's session log; 65 requests in total):

| Time (UTC) | Event | prompt tokens (uncached + cached) | cached |
|---|---|---|---|
| 04:59 → 06:06 | text-only turns | grows 94k → 182k | **hits every turn** (e.g. 181,509 of 182,024) |
| 06:06:22 | browser tool returns the first screenshot (PNG) | — | — |
| 06:08:35 | next request | 183,935 | **0** |
| 06:10:22 | +1 screenshot | 185,536 | **0** |
| 06:12:22 | | 187,499 | **0** |
| 06:14:12 | +1 screenshot | 188,409 | **0** |
| 06:17 → 06:51 | 4 more turns (no new images) | 190k → 200k | **0** every time |

Each of these turns takes ~2 minutes before the first token, because ~190k text tokens that are identical to the previous request are re-prefilled. The images themselves are only ~3 × ≤4,096 tokens near the end of the prompt.

## Cause (as far as I can tell)

Documented and intentional in `docs/vision.md` / `docs/recipes/flash-next-vision.md`: image prompts start from a fresh cache and write no checkpoints, since identical placeholder IDs can stand for different pixels. In code, `engine/family_prefill.py`:

```python
if prepared is not None:
    if start or cache is not None:
        raise ValueError("image prompts require a fresh cache")
    ...
    checkpoints_at = ()
```

So the safety rule also discards the **text prefix before the first image**, which cannot be ambiguous.

## Request

In order of effort:

1. **Reuse the cached prefix up to the first image placeholder** (and allow checkpoints at or before that position). This alone would turn the turns above into ~10–20k-token prefills instead of ~190k.
2. **Include an image content hash in the prefix key** (as vLLM does for multimodal inputs), so prefixes that contain the same images can also be reused and checkpointed after them.

Happy to test a build on the Spark and report numbers.

items.title: Feature request: configurable retained prefix snapshots for Flash Next CUDA
items.body:
Could Flash Next CUDA expose a supported parameter for the number of retained prompt-prefix snapshots, ideally through the existing `--checkpoint-slots` option?

We tested increasing the hardcoded limit from 8 to 16. It substantially reduced response-start latency for one interleaved conversation workload, while a larger workload showed no cache benefit.

### Configuration

- Two independent NVIDIA GB10 / DGX Spark servers with 128 GB unified memory each
- TensorFold v0.6.1, commit `17c73e189f5e6a5304cda7ea37f086f9c49b4788`
- Model: `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP`
- CUDA backend
- `--parallel 16`
- `--context 75000`
- `--kv-dtype int8`
- `--ple-on-ssd`
- `--vision`
- `--mtp-drafts 6`

### Current limitation

The concurrent Flash Next CUDA engine hardcodes `KEEP = 8` in:

`src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/engine.py`

The constant affects both startup memory planning through `indexed_stream_geometry(...)` and runtime retention through `MultiDecoder(..., keep=KEEP)`.

Source:
https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/17c73e189f5e6a5304cda7ea37f086f9c49b4788/src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/engine.py#L15

We applied a local patch to increase this value to 16 on one server, leaving the other at 8 as a comparison server.

### Benchmark results

Requests went directly to the inference servers, bypassing our proxy balancer. These results therefore measure cache retention, not the separate contribution of conversation-affinity routing.

| Workload | Samples per stage | Median time to visible answer: 8 → 16 snapshots | Cached input: 8 → 16 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Six interleaved text conversations | 24 | 3.48 s → 0.27 s | 0% → 99.2% |
| Twelve interleaved text conversations | 48 | 7.78 s → 7.30 s | 0% → 0% |

For six interleaved conversations, median time to visible answer decreased by approximately 92%. The unchanged comparison server remained at approximately 3.51 seconds, supporting a cache-related improvement.

Generation throughput remained approximately 105 tokens/second.

The twelve-conversation workload showed no cache reuse. Its small timing improvement also appeared on the comparison server, so we do not interpret that change as a benefit from increasing retention.

Across the complete benchmark campaign of 496 requests, there were zero errors. The modified server retained at least 27.3 GiB of sampled available memory. This was not a full-capacity stress test.

### Requested behavior

- Expose a configurable retained snapshot count for Flash Next CUDA, preferably through `--checkpoint-slots N`.
- Preserve 8 as the default for compatibility.
- Apply the configured value consistently to startup memory planning and runtime retention.
- Validate the value and report the configured count in startup logs.
- Document the memory tradeoff and interaction with stream capacity.

For example:

`tensorfold serve <model> --backend cuda --parallel 16 --checkpoint-slots 16 ...`

### Why this would help

A supported parameter would let operators tune retention for their available memory and workload without maintaining a source patch.

The results show a substantial benefit when useful text prefixes remain cached, rather than universally faster inference. Snapshot count is not equivalent to conversation count, and additional retention consumes memory.

Would extending the existing parameter to Flash Next CUDA fit the intended design?

items.title: Flash Next CUDA (0.6.1): with --parallel 2, two long conversations never stay resident; a fork may only go into a free slot
items.body:
Thanks for the 0.6.1 message-start states: a new conversation that shares a long system prompt now resumes from it on Flash Next CUDA. On a DGX Spark with a 30,726-token system-and-tools block, the first token now arrives in 3.0 s instead of about 24 s on 0.5.0. That part works as intended.

One gap we measured: **with `--parallel 2` and two long conversations open, neither stays resident.** Every next turn resumes only from the shared system block and re-reads everything after it. Nothing is logged, so the only symptom is first-token time.

### Measured (TensorFold 0.6.1, commit 17c73e18, CUDA, GB10)
Setup:
- a Qwen3.8 Flash Next-family 4-bit MLX MTP build, `--parallel 2 --context 262144 --kv-dtype int8 --mtp-drafts 6 --mtp-confidence 0.60`;
- conversation A of about 50k tokens and conversation B of about 150k tokens, both sharing the 30,726-token system block;
- each next turn adds about 350 tokens;
- thinking off, `max_tokens` 1, three repetitions.

| Next turn | Prompt / cached / seconds |
|---|---|
| A (50k) | 50,239 / **30,726** / 10.2 s (10.2 to 11.4 s over 3 reps) |
| B (150k) | 150,344 / **30,726** / 67.6 s (67.6 to 70.3 s) |

Every next turn of A and B had exactly the system block cached, before anything else interrupted them. The engine reported about 10.7 GiB for caches against about 3.6 GiB needed, and logged no eviction or memory line.

### Cause, from a CPU replay of 0.6.1's own `families/qwen4_exp/cuda/prefixes.py`
We imported `prefixes.py` unchanged, with the message-start points and `multi.py`'s admission rules. The replay reproduced the cached count of 21 of the 23 measured requests (the two misses were stand-in interrupters).
1. A conversation that wants to fork from a shared prefix may fork only into a **free** slot (`prefixes.py:19-20`).
2. The second slot is idle but not free: it still holds an earlier conversation's kept states with a different system prompt. So the conversation resumes in place on the busy slot (`prefixes.py:31-38`), which drops that slot's other entries.
3. A and B therefore take turns in one slot and cut each other back to the system block.

This is not the keep count: in the replay, `KEEP` 16 or 32 changes nothing here. It is related to, but different from, #257, which raises `KEEP` for six or more interleaved conversations.

### What worked in the replay
- A fork rule that may claim the idle slot whose loss forces the fewest tokens to be re-read, instead of only a free slot, keeps A and B resident until something interrupts (`prefixes.py:19-44`).
- With that rule plus `--parallel 3`, they stay resident through an interrupting new task too.
- On 0.5.0 we ran a local patch with the same victim rule: the same two conversations stayed resident at 0.56 s and 0.8 s a turn, with token-identical replies (9 of 9 against fresh prefill).
- Neither change was applied to 0.6.1 or measured on a box.

### Limits
The two-conversation unit ran after another unit in the same boot had put a second system prompt into the other slot. We did not test two long conversations on a boot with no earlier traffic. One model derivative, one box.

The replay script and the per-request counts are available if useful. We can share no prompt or reply text. The same finding is recorded in the community registry as Blackwellboy/model-serving-minefield#169.

items.title: Flash Next (MLX 4-bit + MTP) on a single DGX Spark: v0.6.4 decodes ~24% slower than v0.6.3, with a single stream
items.body:
# Flash Next (MLX 4-bit + MTP) on a single DGX Spark: v0.6.4 decodes ~24 % slower than v0.6.3, with a single stream

**Summary.** On one DGX Spark (GB10, SM 12.1) serving `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP` (MLX 4-bit g32 + MTP,
int8 KV, n-gram tables on SSD), TensorFold **v0.6.4 decodes about 24 % fewer tokens a second than v0.6.3** with the same
weights, the same serve arguments and the same client. The loss is already there with **one** concurrent stream, so it is
not only the multi-stream round planner: whatever changed for a lone stream (v0.6.4 notes call out "a lone stream keeps
its graph slot and captured graphs") costs about a third of single-stream decode.

## Setup (identical for every version compared)

- One DGX Spark, GB10, compute capability 12.1, driver 580.178.04, one CUDA rank.
- Checkpoint `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP` (chat template: the "midsys" Qwen template, identical in all runs).
- `tensorfold serve --parallel 5 --context 262144 --kv-dtype int8 --ple-on-ssd --mtp-drafts 6 --mtp-confidence 0.60`
  (the recipe launcher `MiaAI-Lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Single-DGX-Spark-TensorFold` @ `4c0dea8e`, image built from
  `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.07-py3`, torch 2.13.0a0+9186a08b2c.nv26.07), no local patches.
- Client: OpenAI `/v1/chat/completions`, single stream, 256 output tokens per sample, 5 samples of each kind
  (prose, code, JSON) for the decode median; prefill needle at 2k/8k/32k/64k; concurrency 1/2/4/8/16 with the code prompt.
- Same machine, same day, runs minutes apart, container restarted before each version, GPU 40-45 W, ≤ 65 °C,
  memory headroom ~35 GB.

## Results

| TensorFold | decode median (single stream) | prose | code | JSON | conc. 1 | conc. 4 | conc. 8 | conc. 16 | prefill 32k |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **v0.6.3** | **66.6 t/s** | 50.2 | 68.1 | 68.9 | 63.3 | 129.7 | 127.1 | 131.6 | 1762 t/s |
| **v0.6.4** | **50.8 t/s** | 41.0 | 51.7 | 51.6 | 42.2 | 120.7 | 125.9 | 121.5 | 2309 t/s |

Min/max of the 15 samples, v0.6.3: 48.0-74.7 t/s; v0.6.4: 40.8-54.0 t/s. Prefill is fine (v0.6.4 is even a little faster
there), and the earlier versions are in the same band as v0.6.3: v0.6.0 67.7 t/s, v0.6.2 66.0 t/s.

**Control with the quick profile** (single stream, 3 samples per kind, ~1 min per version) to rule out the neighbouring
variables:

| build | decode median |
|---|---:|
| v0.6.2 with the MiaAI recipe patch applied | 63.2 t/s |
| v0.6.2 **without** any patch | 65.5 t/s |
| v0.6.3 without any patch | 65.6 t/s |
| v0.6.4 without any patch | **39.5 t/s** |

So the recipe's patch is not the cause (removing it changes nothing), and the regression tracks the engine version:
it appears in v0.6.4 and not in v0.6.3.

## Reproduction

```bash
pip install "git+https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold@v0.6.4"     # and @v0.6.3 for the comparison
tensorfold serve Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP \
  --name qwen3.8-flash-next-mlx4-mtp-tensorfold --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --parallel 5 --context 262144 --kv-dtype int8 --ple-on-ssd \
  --mtp-drafts 6 --mtp-confidence 0.60 --thinking
# then, for the single-stream number: POST /v1/chat/completions with max_tokens=256, stream=false,
# and read the client-side tok/s over 5 samples of each kind (prose, code, JSON).
```

## Guess at the cause (not verified)

v0.6.4 is the release where `--parallel N` learned to run across two CUDA ranks in shared lane rounds (#141), and its
notes say a lone stream keeps its graph slot and captured graphs. On one rank with `--parallel 5` the lone-stream path is
already 33 % slower (63.3 -> 42.2 t/s at concurrency 1), while prefill and the multi-stream aggregates move much less
(conc. 8 is 127.1 -> 125.9). A per-request logging or metrics line cannot explain 12 t/s. If it helps, I can test a build
with a flag, bisect the commits between v0.6.3 and v0.6.4 on this machine, or run any diagnostic you want (metrics,
`/health`, capture with Nsight, `tensorfold plan` output) and report back with numbers.

Happy to keep the machine available for whatever you need; I can reproduce both numbers on request.

| Prefill-heavy | 79.6 | 83.0 | 4.3% |

Both versions used the same 4-bit weights, int8 KV, 75k context, MTP settings (6 drafts / 0.60 confidence), and custom KEEP32 setting. CUDA Graph configuration was unchanged.

items.title: CUDA Flash Next: prefix cache stops matching at 3 or more concurrent requests; one-token throughput drops by 60 %
items.body:
**Version:** TensorFold v0.6.5 (pip `tensorfold 0.6.5`, no local patches), in a container on the NGC PyTorch 26.07 image. One DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB).

**Server flags:**
`serve Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 --parallel 5 --context 262144 --kv-dtype int8 --mtp-drafts 6 --mtp-confidence 0.60 --temperature 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --max-tokens 32768 --thinking`
Environment: `TENSORFOLD_PREFILL_ROWS=2048`, `TENSORFOLD_MTP_COPY=1`, `TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_RESERVE_GIB=2`.

**Workload:** yes/no classification. Each request has the same system message (about 540 tokens) and a different short user message (about 80 tokens). Total prompt: 622 tokens. Request fields: `max_tokens: 1`, `temperature: 0`, `logprobs: true`, `top_logprobs: 20`, `chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false}`. Each client sends its next request when the previous reply arrives. 200 requests for each level, 3 runs for each level. The values are medians of the 3 runs.

**Result:**

| Concurrent requests | Requests/s | Median latency (s) | Mean server TTFT (s) | Median `prefill_s` | Median `cached_tokens` | Requests with a cache hit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4.58 | 0.22 | 0.19 | 0.110 | 540 | 100 % |
| 2 | 5.27 | 0.37 | 0.35 | 0.108 | 540 | 99 % |
| 3 | 2.12 | 1.46 | 1.37 | 0.323 | 0 | 1-3 % |
| 4 | 2.59 | 1.49 | 1.47 | 0.307 | 0 | 12-17 % |
| 5 | 2.77 | 1.80 | 1.54 | 0.278 | 0 | 10-20 % |

(Cache-hit share comes from the `--mtp-drafts 0` run. The `--mtp-drafts 6` runs give the same median `cached_tokens` and the same cache-hit share.)

**What we see:**
1. From 2 to 3 concurrent requests, throughput decreases from 5.27 to 2.12 requests/s.
2. At the same step, the shared prefix stops matching. `cached_tokens` decreases from 540 to 0, and `prefill_s` increases 3 times.
3. At all levels, throughput follows 1 / (`prefill_s` + about 0.1 s), and mean TTFT is about N × (`prefill_s` + 0.1 s). Prompt passes run one at a time. The only change at 3 requests is the cache miss, which makes each prompt pass 3 times longer.
4. MTP is not the cause. `mtp_drafted_total` stays at 0 for all 3,000 requests (a one-token reply has no decode round). With `--mtp-drafts 0`, the results are the same within 5 %.

**Expected:** the shared system message stays in the prefix cache at all concurrency levels up to `--parallel`, and throughput does not decrease when concurrency increases. (Batched prompt passes for short prompts are a separate improvement; this ticket is about the cache miss.)

**Questions:**
1. Why does the shared prefix stop matching at 3 concurrent requests?
2. Is there a setting that keeps a shared system block for all streams?

**Related:** #257 (configurable retained prefix snapshots). Our case is different: the cache works at 1–2 concurrent requests and stops matching at 3.

**Settings that do not change the result:** two defaults have the value 3, so we tested them. With `--max-snapshots 8`, with `--checkpoint-slots 8`, and with both at 8, the result at 3 concurrent requests is the same: 2.07 to 2.20 requests/s, and only 1 % to 7 % of requests get a cache hit. At 5 concurrent requests, about 1 request in 5 gets a cache hit in all runs. Free memory stays above 32 GiB in all runs, so memory pressure is probably not the cause.

**Minor:** with `--mtp-drafts 0`, the startup log says "no drafts: the serial reference", but the "serving" line says "drafts: on" and each reply has `"drafts": true`.

**Repro:** a self-contained Python script (standard library only) that makes the synthetic prompts and runs the levels. We can attach it.

items.title: GLM on CUDA: an opt-in FP8 or 4-bit latent cache (`--kv-dtype fp8` / `fp4`), lossy, with paired quality results on full GLM-5.3
items.body:
## What

An opt-in, lossy format for GLM's per-token latent cache on CUDA. The default stays bf16 and keeps its bits.
CONTRIBUTING says a precision mode is a separate conversation, so we are asking before any pull request.

- **fp8:** each 512-wide latent row as e4m3 codes with one power-of-two scale.
- **fp4:** e2m1 codes, an e4m3 scale per 16 values, and the same power-of-two row scale.

This overlaps #309, where @Bizuayeu proposes the FP8 form for GLM-5.3-Flash, adapted from our Flash recipe's
[`0038-glm-kv-fp8`](https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold/blob/main/patches/0038-glm-kv-fp8.patch).
The FP8 row format is the same. This issue adds what we have built and measured since, on full GLM-5.3 (#402): the 4-bit form, paired quality runs, and a proposal for how
the formats could be exposed. If you would rather keep one thread, we can move this into #309.

## Why

The latent cache is replicated on every rank, because all heads read the same latent. It does not shrink with more
ranks, so on unified-memory machines it is what limits the window. Full GLM-5.3 has 78 MLA layers, and 21 of them
run the indexer. Bytes a token on each rank, without the MTP layer:

| Format | Latent row (512 values) | Rotary key (64) | Index key (128, 21 layers) | A token a rank |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| bf16 | 1,024 | 128 | 256 | 95,232 |
| fp8 | 528 | 128 (bf16) | 256 (bf16) | 56,544 |
| fp4 | 304 | 128 (bf16) | 256 (bf16) | 39,072 |

On three DGX Sparks without context parallelism, fp8 admits a 163,840-token window (boot p3). In the same memory,
bf16 would hold about 97k tokens (computed, not booted). With context parallelism, which we list in the full-model
issue as a follow-up, fp4 holds 499,712 tokens (boot cp500b). At a 655,360-token window, fp4 freed about 3.6 GiB a
Spark compared with fp8.

## The formats

- **fp8.** A row's scale is 2^(ceil(log2 amax) - 8), so the row's largest value quantizes into [128, 256], below
  e4m3's 448, and nothing saturates. The fp32 scale sits in a 16-byte pad after the codes, so rows stay aligned and the
  engine's existing row handling (slices, clones, kept snapshots) works unchanged. Readers convert the codes to bf16,
  which is exact, and fold the scale into their fp32 products, which is exact for a power of two.
- **fp4.** Two codes a byte. Each 16-value block's scale is its amax / 6 over the row scale, rounded to e4m3. A code
  times its block scale is exact in bf16, so readers dequantize to bf16 and fold the row's power of two in as with fp8.
- **Rotary and index keys stay bf16** in both formats, as DeepSeek's FP8 MLA cache keeps its rotary part in bf16.
- Our recipe also has an opt-in `fp4x`
  ([0133](https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-EXL3-3x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold/blob/main/patches/0133-glm-full-kv-fp4x.patch),
  [0137](https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-EXL3-3x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold/blob/main/patches/0137-glm-full-kv-fp4x-fix.patch)).
  It stores the rotary and index keys as e4m3 too, at 31,476 bytes a token, and gives about 24% more tokens than fp4.
  Its e4m3 codes come from one integer encoder (round to nearest even on the fp32 bits, saturating at 448), never a
  hardware conversion, in both the kernels and the torch definition. We do not propose `fp4x` here: see Quality.

## What stays exact

A row's bytes depend on its own bf16 row and nothing else. One writer helper quantizes the rows of both prompt chunks
and decode windows. The readers dequantize exactly and then run the bf16 arithmetic. At the same format:

- a drafted reply equals `"draft": false`;
- a resumed prompt equals a fresh one;
- any prompt chunking leaves the same cache;
- graphs equal eager.

Replies differ from bf16's.

Measured with our `tools/exact.py` (drafted against `"draft": false`, and requests sent together against each sent
alone, greedy and seeded sampling): 12/12 on fp8 boots (p3, p17, p19) and on fp4 boots (fp4g655, hcp). The tests check
four things. The write kernels store the torch definition byte for byte. A reader on a quantized cache equals the same
reader on a bf16 cache that holds the dequantized rows. Drafted windows equal serial steps, on a tiny random GLM-5.3
checkpoint in the real layout. Graphs equal eager on the GPU.

## Quality

We ran a fixed, seeded suite with checkable answers (greedy). Boot fp8g393 (fp8) and boot fp4g655 (fp4) ran the same
items. The p values are from an exact two-sided McNemar test on the items that only one format got right:

| Category | fp8 | fp4 | Only fp8 right | Only fp4 right | p |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Short questions, thinking off | 123/150 | 124/150 | 6 | 7 | 1.00 |
| Chained arithmetic (10 steps), thinking on | 40/40 | 39/40 | 1 | 0 | 1.00 |
| Ledger tracking (25 transfers), thinking on | 35/40 | 35/40 | 4 | 4 | 1.00 |
| Python tasks against hidden tests | 25/25 | 25/25 | 0 | 0 | 1.00 |

Every ledger miss, in both runs, was a reply that ran past the 12,288-token limit, and every finished reply was right.
The texts differ: a lossy cache moves a near tie early, and greedy decoding then takes another path. Recall of 16 keys
(4 corrected later) with fp4: 112/112 keys, none stale, at about 39k, 157k and 314k tokens. With fp4, needles were
correct at 9.9k, 94k and 314k tokens.

`fp4x` against fp4 (boot fp4x500) was equal on short questions (124/150 each), arithmetic and Python. Ledger tracking
gave 31/40 against 35/40 (p 0.34). That is not significant, but it leans toward fp4: fp4x ran past the limit 8 times
(fp4: 5) and gave one wrong finished answer. That is why we would leave it out.

**Not measured yet:** a paired bf16 against fp8 run on full GLM-5.3, and a clean speed A/B between the formats. We
would add both to the receipt: the suite at bf16, fp8 and fp4 on one build, and `bench_openai.py` and
`prefill_cold.py` before and after.

## Proposal

- **Flag.** `--kv-dtype` already exists for Flash Next (#47), and a family declares what it serves
  (`CUDA_KV_DTYPES`, checked in `serve_options.py`). We would add `fp8` and `fp4` as values. GLM-5.3-Flash would
  declare `("bf16", "fp8")` and full GLM-5.3 `("bf16", "fp8", "fp4")`. Every other family and the MLX path refuse
  them, as they refuse `int8` today. The ranks compare the value at startup and refuse to start on a mismatch.
- **Names.** We would keep these apart from `int8` / `int4`, which are ExLlamaV3's Hadamard-rotated groups with fp16
  scales. These are float codes with power-of-two row scales and no rotation.
- **Code.** A new `families/glm5_next/cuda/kv8.py` would hold the formats, their torch definition and the Triton
  store and load helpers. The latent writer and the absorbed and sparse attention readers go in `latent.py`.
  GLM-5.3-Flash's pooled index keys go in `sparse.py` (FP8 only, as in #309). The cache bytes go in
  `cuda/geometry.py`, so admission counts the smaller rows. Full GLM-5.3's readers (`dsa_full.py`) come with that
  family.
- **Kept prompt states** carry their format. A state saved in one format is never read in another.

## What we would submit, in order

1. FP8 for GLM-5.3-Flash: if #309 goes ahead, we would review and test it on our Sparks rather than open a second
   pull request.
2. FP8 for full GLM-5.3, after that family lands with bf16 as its only cache.
3. FP4 for full GLM-5.3
   ([0115](https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-EXL3-3x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold/blob/main/patches/0115-glm-full-kv-fp4.patch)),
   with the paired bf16 / fp8 / fp4 receipt.
4. `fp4x` only if you want it.

## Platforms

CUDA only. Measured on three DGX Sparks (GB10, 128 GB each). The FP8 form for GLM-5.3-Flash ran on two and three
Sparks in our Flash recipe. Not run on an RTX PRO 6000 (full GLM-5.3 does not fit on one) or on Macs (#381 asks for a
quantized cache on MLX separately).

## Questions

1. Would you take a lossy latent cache as an explicit opt-in, as Flash Next's `--kv-dtype int8` is? Or only as a
   mode that a checkpoint turns on (#309's `kv_cache_scheme` question)? Our checkpoint declares no KV scheme.
2. `--kv-dtype fp8` / `fp4`, or other names?
3. What quality evidence do you want for a lossy cache? Is a paired suite with McNemar tests and needles enough?
4. One thread with #309, or two?

## Credit

The FP8 row format and its readers come from our Flash recipe's patch 0038 (Mia's AI Lab, Apache 2.0), which #309
adapts. Keeping the rotary part in bf16 beside an FP8 latent follows DeepSeek's FP8 MLA cache (DeepSeek-V3.2, by
DeepSeek-AI). That is the design only: no DeepSeek code is used. The 4-bit formats are ours.

The full recipe is [MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-EXL3-3x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold](https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-EXL3-3x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold)
(Apache 2.0, patches on TensorFold v0.6.0). Each figure above names its boot there.

items.title: feat(mlx): support quantized KV cache (--kv-dtype int8/int4) on Apple Silicon
items.body:
### Feature Request / Proposal

Currently, attempting to start TensorFold on macOS with `--kv-dtype int4` or `int8` returns:
```text
tensorfold: --kv-dtype int4 is a CUDA engine option: the MLX path caches keys and values as bf16
```

### Context & Motivation
On Apple Silicon unified memory machines (such as 16 GB, 24 GB, or 32 GB M1/M2/M3/M4 Macs), large models like `Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit` reside with ~15–16 GB weights + drafter ~3.8 GB, leaving ~7–10 GB headroom.
Under full `bf16` KV cache, long context windows or multi-turn conversations quickly exhaust resident memory budget and severely limit parallel requests or context scaling.

### Proposed Solution
Add support for quantized KV caching (`int8` / `int4` group-quantized or scale-quantized keys & values) on the Apple Silicon / MLX backend:
- Leverage MLX's quantized KV cache capabilities (`mlx.core.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention` with quantized K/V cache or equivalent Metal lane kernel).
- Allow `--kv-dtype int8` and `--kv-dtype int4` on the MLX backend.

This would dramatically increase allowable context length on Apple Silicon devices and bring parity with the existing CUDA engine features.

items.title: Flash Next (CUDA): keep a state at message starts so new conversations that share a system prompt can resume, as the 27B path does
items.body:
**Setup**
- TensorFold 0.5.0, and 0.6.0 (c4646171), on CUDA with one DGX Spark (GB10).
- A Flash Next MLX 4-bit checkpoint with its MTP head: `--parallel 5` (also measured at `--parallel 1`), `--context 262144 --kv-dtype int8 --mtp-drafts 6`.
- For comparison, Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 with DFlash2 at `--parallel 2`, on the same machine with the same prompts.

**Workload**
Agent traffic. Every request starts with the same block of about 30.7k tokens (a long system prompt plus 36 tool schemas), and conversations differ only after it. In our prompts the first differing token is at 30,759, and whole prompts are about 35.7k tokens.

**Observed**
Measured from `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` and wall time, with `max_tokens` 1, thinking off, and a clean cache:

| | New conversation that shares the block | Next turn of the same conversation |
|---|---|---|
| Flash Next, 0.5.0 and 0.6.0, `--parallel` 1 and 5 | 0 cached, about 23.5 s (the whole ~35.7k is prefilled again) | about 35.7k cached, 0.24 s |
| Qwen3.8-27B, 0.5.0 and 0.6.0 | 30,726 cached, about 4.2 s (resumes at the message start) | about 35.7k cached, 0.4 s |

On 0.6.0 the 27B with `--checkpoint-slots 8` also keeps full-prompt resume for two conversations that interleave.

**Cause, as we read it in the source** (0.5.0, `families/qwen4_exp/cuda/multi.py`)
The concurrent decoder remembers only each admitted prompt's end (`_remember(list(s.prompt), ...)`). `_slot_for` resumes only when a new prompt extends one of those kept prompts. Prefill does not keep states at message starts, the way the 27B engine does (`resume_points` plus the `_stops` / `keep` callback in `families/qwen3_5/cuda/engine.py`). So a new conversation that shares only the system and tools block can never resume.

**Request**
For Flash Next on CUDA, keep a state at detected message starts (at least the end of the system and tools block) as the 27B path does, with a slot setting like `--checkpoint-slots`. For agent workloads at this prompt size, that would cut time-to-first-token for each new conversation from about 23 s to about 4 s.

**Offer**
We can test a branch on a DGX Spark and report:
- token identity of resumed against fresh replies (`token_sha`);
- cached counts and timings;
- resend and next-turn behaviour.
We would also be glad to attempt a PR, if you would welcome one.

items.title: [CUDA] prefix retention does not engage on the CUDA lane: re-sending an identical context still costs a full prefill
items.body:
**Environment**
- 1x DGX Spark (GB10, SM121), TensorFold **0.3.6.3**, CUDA lane
- Model: `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP` (Flash Next, MLX 4-bit)
- Launch: `tensorfold serve <model> --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --context 262144 --parallel 4 --kv-dtype int8 --checkpoint-slots 16 --prompt-cache-gib 8 --snapshot-dir /hostlogs/tf-snapshots`
- Startup line: `CUDA rank 0 startup estimate 96.84 GiB within 104.94 GiB; native 262144, allocated prompt/reply window 262144, cache slots 262151`

**What works well on this lane** (measured on the same box): prefill ~1,597 tok/s at a 1K prompt and ~2,339 tok/s at ~4K; 4 concurrent streams aggregate **92.7 tok/s** with every reply equal to its solo run; and 0.3.6.3 lets a full **262144** window fit on CUDA (0.3.6.1 refused 262144 and capped out at ~226,981).

**What does not work: prefix retention across turns.** With a real multi-turn conversation (each turn appending ~25 tokens), every turn pays a full prefill — and re-sending a **byte-identical** context costs exactly as much as a fresh one:

| turn | prompt_tokens | prefill wall (`max_tokens=1`) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 15,061 | 6.37 s |
| 2 | 15,086 | 6.39 s |
| 3 | 15,112 | 6.44 s |
| **control: resend the identical context** | 15,123 | **6.44 s** |

15,061 tokens ÷ 6.44 s ≈ **2,340 tok/s**, i.e. the full prefill rate — no reuse. The same shape holds at ~2.3K (1.11 → 1.14 s per turn, and 1.15 s for the identical resend). The server log contains **no** snapshot / prefix / checkpoint lines at all during these runs, so the retention machinery appears not to engage on this lane.

**Why it matters to us.** #68 added the retention + spill + `--checkpoint-slots` machinery and validated it on MLX (its notes say `tests/cuda` was not run); #72 describes exactly our shape — a shared system block with only the ~20-token tails prefilled. Our workload is a fixed ~20K system prompt with pure-append turns (a coding agent loop). On this box, llama.cpp reuses that prefix at **0.10 s** TTFT for the same shape, and that single property is what currently keeps us on the other engine for multi-turn work; TensorFold's prefill is ~3x faster per turn, so if retention worked here it would be the better engine outright.

**Ask**
1. Is prefix retention supposed to work on the CUDA lane today (i.e. are we missing a flag, or should `--prompt-cache-gib` / `--checkpoint-slots` / `--snapshot-dir` apply here as they do on MLX)?
2. If it is MLX-only for now, is CUDA retention on the roadmap? We are happy to run test builds and report numbers — including the multi-turn control test above, which is cheap to reproduce.

Happy to provide the launch script and raw logs if useful.
